title: Proving you are human
text: Every time you click a box that says 'I am not a robot', you are {{1}} in an argument that machines are slowly winning. The idea is simple: set a task that humans find {{2}} and computers find hard, and only people will pass. The first generation asked users to {{3}} distorted words — a test computers initially failed — and the results were put to work: those fuzzy words came from old books being digitised, so each answer {{4}} an archive. But machine learning improved faster than the puzzles did, and by 2014 software could {{5}} distorted text more reliably than people. The designers adapted rather than surrendered: newer versions watch how you move the mouse, how you {{6}} with the page — dozens of tiny signals that humans produce without thinking. It is a strange {{7}} of security: the proof of humanity is no longer what you know but how naturally you behave, and the moment machines learn to behave naturally too, the test will need {{8}} again. For now, the little checkbox quietly settles the question billions of times a day, and usually gets it right.

gaps.explanation: 'you are caught in an argument that machines are slowly winning' — trapped in it; taught, carried and housed do not express entanglement.
'humans find easy and computers find hard' — the adjective is needed after 'find'; easily is the adverb.
'asked users to type distorted words' — key them in; tile = cover with tiles, tote = carry.
'each answer enriched an archive' — added value to it; entitle = give a right to, enlist = join up.
'software could interpret distorted text' — make sense of it; interrogate = question a suspect.
'how you interact with the page' — act and react with it; interject = interrupt with a remark.
'a strange definition of security' — an odd way of defining it; delegation = a group of representatives.
'the test will need reinventing again' — will have to be created anew; remunerate = pay.
